title: The Wagons Beneath the Borrowed Capital
summary: A priest-general’s mobile defenses and a wealthy craft dynasty operate amid competing military governments and long-lived migrant kingdoms.
source_notes: A priest continuing religious service while commanding radical forces becomes a wagon general with overlapping roles.
Concentrated dynastic craft wealth and influential eccentric fashion become a cart-building household and copied dress customs; industrial manufacture is excluded.
Military factions retaining external recognition, loans, and customs access become rival capital offices whose formal legitimacy exceeds actual control.
Long-lived kingdoms formed through warrior migration and intermarriage become a pasture confederation adapting beneath successive outside administrations.

entries.title: Proven of the Wagon Prayer
entries.body:
Proven conducted finite rites before inspecting wagon joints. Opponents called his roles incompatible. His account distinguishes ritual witness from mechanical safety, showing that combining professions need not mean treating sacred authority as proof a wheel will hold.

Later accounts make Proven of the Wagon Prayer the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Wagons Beneath the Borrowed Capital. A confederation of pasture kingdoms formed through migration and intermarriage, retaining local rulers even under later outside administrations. In 932 a priest-general organized defensive wagons while continuing ritual duties, unsettling households accustomed to separating those roles. A wealthy cart-building dynasty supplied repairs and adopted eccentric dress copied as aristocratic taste. Competing generals claimed one capital, obtaining foreign recognition, loans, and customs income despite incomplete local control. The pasture kingdoms negotiated with whichever office could actually sustain a route. Present descendants inherit useful wagon techniques alongside exaggerated accounts of a single commanding state, making continuity a question of maintenance, marriage, and finite commitments rather than unchanged political unity.

In the connected record, [The Borrowed Capital Custom House](b038-the-borrowed-capital-custom-house.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Benefited Repair Assessment](b038-the-benefited-repair-assessment.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: which recognized capital office should repay repairs ordered by rivals when every current claimant benefited from the routes kept open.

entries.title: The Borrowed Capital Custom House
entries.body:
Rival seals appear on consecutive toll receipts issued from the same desk. Outside merchants accepted each when useful. Local carriers seek refunds for duplicated fees, grounding legitimacy’s grand contest in costs the supposedly continuous government actually imposed.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Pasture Kingdom Council
entries.body:
Kingdoms share roads while preserving local succession rules. Outside administrations retained those structures for convenience. Their survival records adaptation and unequal bargains, rather than proving either untouched autonomy or complete disappearance under conquest.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Capital Without the Roads
entries.body:
A general gained recognition and credit while rival forces controlled approach routes. His orders created debts he could not fulfill directly. Present claimants invoke his prestige but resist responsibility for the supplies obtained through that same recognition.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Cart Lord’s Glove Ring
entries.body:
A wealthy patron wore a ring over his glove, and courtiers copied the inconvenience. Carpenters used the style to identify ceremonial visitors unfamiliar with work. The custom’s prestige spread while its practical absurdity became an understated local joke.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Joint Inspected After Prayer
entries.body:
Crews test every wagon after rites instead of treating blessing as sufficient. The practice protects both finite ritual and ordinary skill. Patrons object when inspection delays ceremony, revealing which form of confidence they value more than actual safety.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Kingdoms’ Marriage Routes
entries.body:
The record follows marriages and migration between pasture courts. Later pedigrees simplify mixed origins into one heroic descent. Keeping the routes visible preserves cooperation and specific ancestors without requiring every present household to claim an unmixed founding people.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Wagon Brake Grasshopper
entries.body:
Large grasshoppers gather in warm stored wheel spokes and damage bindings. Crews inspect them before travel. Soldiers once called infestations enemy curses, while carpenters recognize the storage conditions that make preventable harm likely.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Recognized Customs Circuit
entries.body:
Merchants carried receipts among rival offices seeking whichever would honor them. The circuit reduced some losses and encouraged duplicated demands. Its surviving papers expose practical negotiation beneath the claim that international recognition established one functioning jurisdiction everywhere.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Benefited Repair Assessment
entries.body:
A repair debt may be assessed against documented beneficiaries when the ordering office vanishes. The clause requires evidence, not mere resemblance of titles. It prevents rival successors enjoying maintained roads while all denying any connection to the costs.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The First Moving Defense
entries.body:
Wagons provided cover and carried provisions but became dangerous when crews ignored terrain. Victory accounts erase stuck wheels. Repair logs preserve failures that make the technique teachable instead of a legendary device imagined to work independently of labor and place.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Four Sealed Axle Bill
entries.body:
Four rival offices endorsed one repair bill. Each now claims the others should pay. The document proves shared authorization but not equal benefit, requiring actual route and cargo accounts before a fair assessment can be made.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Local Ruler Named Twice
entries.body:
Announcements give a ruler’s inherited title and current negotiated duty. The practice preserves dignity while identifying actual scope. It counters outside summaries that treat a surviving court either as sovereign in every matter or merely decorative.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Borrowed Capital Loans
entries.body:
The ledger links external credit to customs receipts collected locally. Some loans funded useful repairs; others funded rival campaigns. Readers separate uses, giving repayment claims a practical basis stronger than either unconditional continuity or blanket repudiation.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Wheels Turning at Rest
entries.body:
One wagon wheel moves slightly when a promised repair meal is withheld. An uneven floor explains some motion but not every recurrence. Crews fulfill the finite provisioning duty while inspecting the object, refusing to turn a local effect into a general military omen.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Wagon Axle Seasoning
entries.body:
Axles dry slowly and require timber chosen for strength, not prestige. Rushed commissions fail. Craft witnesses publish realistic schedules, making the dynasty’s useful knowledge accessible beyond the patrons who can afford its fastest ceremonial promises.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Capital Repair Inheritance
entries.body:
Successor offices claim recognized authority but disown repairs ordered during factional rule. Carriers demand a benefit-based inquiry. The settlement must identify who can provide actual repayment rather than award an elegant historical title whose holder has no usable stores.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
